a: Frank Lloyd Wright (1867-1959) was an American architect who pioneered organic architecture, the philosophy that buildings should harmonize with their environment. His most iconic works include Fallingwater (1935), a house built dramatically over a waterfall in Pennsylvania that exemplifies the integration of structure and nature, and the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in New York City (1959), with its distinctive spiral ramp gallery. Wright also designed the Robie House in Chicago, the Johnson Wax Headquarters in Wisconsin, and Taliesin, his own home and school in Wisconsin. He developed the Usonian house concept, affordable homes for the American middle class characterized by open floor plans, natural materials, and radiant floor heating.

Le Corbusier (1887-1965), born Charles-Edouard Jeanneret in Switzerland, was a pioneering modernist architect, urban planner, and writer whose five points of architecture became foundational principles of modern design: pilotis (columns), roof garden, open floor plan, ribbon windows, and free facade. His seminal works include the Villa Savoye in Poissy, France (1931), a pure expression of these principles; the Unite d'Habitation in Marseille (1952), a mixed-use residential block that influenced brutalist housing worldwide; and the Chapel of Notre Dame du Haut in Ronchamp (1954), a dramatic departure from his earlier rationalist style. He developed the Modulor, a system of proportions based on the human scale, and profoundly influenced urban planning with his concept of the Radiant City.

Antoni Gaudi (1852-1926) was a Catalan architect known for his highly individualistic style that blended Art Nouveau, Gothic Revival, and his own organic, nature-inspired forms. His magnum opus is the Basilica of the Sagrada Familia in Barcelona, a colossal church under construction since 1882 that combines Gothic and curvilinear Art Nouveau forms with intricate facades depicting biblical scenes. Other major works include Casa Batllo (1906), a residential building with a skeletal facade and colorful trencadis (broken tile mosaic); Casa Mila (1912), a undulating stone building with iron balconies; and Park Guell, a public park featuring serpentine benches covered in vibrant mosaic. Seven of Gaudi's works are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, and his distinctive style continues to inspire architects worldwide.

Zaha Hadid (1950-2016) was an Iraqi-British architect who became the first woman to receive the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2004. Known for her fluid, futuristic forms and parametric design approach, she created buildings characterized by sweeping curves, dynamic lines, and dramatic cantilevers. Her major works include the Heydar Aliyev Center in Baku, Azerbaijan (2012), a flowing white structure that appears to rise from the ground like a wave; the MAXXI National Museum of 21st Century Arts in Rome; the Guangzhou Opera House in China; the London Aquatics Centre for the 2012 Olympics; and the Bergisel Ski Jump in Innsbruck, Austria. Hadid's style, often called parametrism, uses digital design and fabrication to create complex geometries that challenge traditional architectural conventions.

Several other architects have left an indelible mark on modern architecture. Frank Gehry (born 1929) revolutionized deconstructivism with the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao (1997), whose titanium-clad curves sparked the Bilbao effect. I.M. Pei (1917-2019) masterfully blended modernist geometry with cultural context, designing the Louvre Pyramid in Paris and the Bank of China Tower in Hong Kong. Louis Sullivan (1856-1924), mentor to Frank Lloyd Wright, pioneered the skyscraper with his Wainwright Building and coined form follows function. Ludwig Mies van der Rohe (1886-1969) championed minimalist steel-and-glass architecture with the Barcelona Pavilion and Seagram Building. Alvar Aalto (1898-1976) brought humanistic organic forms to modernism with works like the Finlandia Hall. Renzo Piano (born 1937) designed the Centre Pompidou in Paris and the Shard in London, known for high-tech expressive structures.
